title: Backcasting from 'Eval Benchmarks Aren't Contaminated': Probing Training-Data Contamination of a Governance-Relevant Benchmark

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Eval Benchmarks Aren't Contaminated': Probing Training-Data Contamination of a Governance-Relevant Benchmark

**Problem:** A success state where governance relies on benchmark scores requires those benchmarks not be contaminated (memorized from training data), which inflates apparent capability and corrupts threshold/risk decisions. Contamination is plausible but rarely checked for governance-relevant evals.

**Direction:** On a small open model, apply standard contamination-detection heuristics (e.g., comparing performance on canonical vs perturbed/reworded benchmark items, or n-gram overlap probes against public corpora) to one widely-used capability benchmark. Quantify evidence of memorization and estimate how much it could inflate a governance threshold decision.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'benchmark-based governance is sound' shows contamination-freedom as the precondition. Demonstrating contamination in a governance-relevant benchmark warns regulators that compute/capability thresholds resting on it may be mis-set. Small open model + public corpora; a methodologically clean outsider experiment.

**Relevant context:** 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (arXiv:2601.23112) on benchmark quality; Benchrisk identified 57 benchmark failure modes; Epoch capability tracking underpins threshold debates. Contamination-detection literature (perturbation/n-gram methods).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain but contamination corrupting governance thresholds requires several steps; the catastrophic link is indirect.
